Task 1: NLP Fundamentals, Pipeline & Data Exploration¶

  • Objective: Establish the theoretical foundations of Natural Language Processing, map the end-to-end NLP pipeline to our airline sentiment task, and inspect real-world dataset properties including class imbalance and linguistic challenges.
  • Expected Output: Conceptual tables and pipeline diagram, dataset shape/null/duplicate summary, 3 EDA plots, and 5 real challenge tweets from Tweets.csv.

1.1 What is NLP and Why Do We Need It?¶

Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a branch of artificial intelligence and computational linguistics that enables computers to read, interpret, and generate human language in a meaningful way. Computers natively understand structured numeric data, whereas human communication—emails, support tickets, tweets, and voice transcripts—is unstructured, ambiguous, and produced at massive scale every second. Without automated NLP systems, organisations cannot manually analyse millions of customer messages or extract timely insights from text streams.

Five important real-world applications of NLP include:

  1. Search Engines: Understanding user query intent, synonyms, and spelling variations to retrieve relevant web pages.
  2. Spam Filtering: Automatically classifying incoming emails into spam or inbox using word patterns and sender signals.
  3. Customer-Support Chatbots (Indian Use Case): Conversational bots used by Indian fintech and telecom platforms (such as UPI banking assistants on WhatsApp) to resolve balance, transaction, and KYC queries in English and Hinglish.
  4. Machine Translation (Indian Use Case): India's Bhashini initiative and regional e-governance portals translate public services and educational content across 22 scheduled Indian languages (such as Hindi, Tamil, Gujarati, and Bengali).
  5. Customer-Review & Social Media Analysis: E-commerce marketplaces and airlines monitor customer tweets and product reviews in real time to detect service outages and measure customer satisfaction.

1.2 Common NLP Tasks and Approach Families¶

NLP Task One-Line Description Concrete Example
Text Classification Assigning one or more predefined category labels to an entire document. Routing an airline tweet to Baggage, Delay, or Billing.
Sentiment Analysis Detecting whether the opinion expressed in text is positive, negative, or neutral. Classifying "Flight delayed 4 hours, awful service" as negative.
Named-Entity Recognition (NER) Identifying and labelling real-world entities such as organisations, people, and places. Extracting United Airlines (ORG) and Chicago (LOC) from a tweet.
Part-of-Speech (POS) Tagging Labelling each word with its grammatical role (noun, verb, adjective, etc.). Tagging "delayed" as a verb (VBN/VBD) or adjective (JJ).
Machine Translation Converting text automatically from one human language to another while preserving meaning. Translating an English flight alert into Hindi or Gujarati.
Summarisation Condensing a long document or thread into a concise summary preserving key facts. Turning 500 customer complaints into a 3-bullet daily operations brief.
Question Answering Finding or generating a direct answer to a natural-language question from context. Answering "What is the baggage allowance?" from airline policy text.

Three NLP Approach Families Covered in This Practical¶

Approach Family How It Works Example in PR 1
Heuristic (Rules & Lexicons) Uses hand-crafted word lists and explicit rules (such as negation flipping). Domain positive/negative airline lexicon + 2-word negation check (Task 3.2).
API-Based (Ready-Made Service) Sends raw text to an external or pre-built engine and reads back a sentiment score. NLTK VADER compound polarity scoring; similar in pattern to Cloud NLP APIs (Task 3.3).
Machine-Learning-Based Extracts numeric feature vectors (BoW, TF-IDF, N-grams, Word2Vec) and learns weights from labelled training data. Logistic Regression / Linear SVC / Naive Bayes inside a scikit-learn Pipeline (Tasks 4–6).

Class Imbalance Observation (Task 1.5):
The dataset is heavily imbalanced: roughly 63% of tweets are negative, 21% are neutral, and only 16% are positive. Because a naive model that predicts negative for every tweet would still achieve ~63% accuracy while completely failing on neutral and positive feedback, accuracy alone is misleading. We therefore use Macro-F1 (which weights all three classes equally) as our primary evaluation metric alongside per-class precision and recall.

Task 2: Text Cleaning with RegEx & Tokenisation¶

  • Objective: Design, test, and apply Regular Expression (RegEx) cleaning rules and negation-preserving stop-word removal, then inspect vocabulary statistics to guide feature extraction.
  • Expected Output: RegEx pattern tests and summary table, clean_text column, stop-word comparison on 'not happy with the delay', and top-15 token plots per sentiment class.

2.1 Cleaning Rules & Trade-offs¶

We apply the following cleaning steps in strict order:

  1. Lowercase (text.lower()): Merges "Flight", "FLIGHT", and "flight" into a single token.
  2. Remove URLs (https?://\S+): Strips web links (http://t.co/...) before punctuation removal destroys :// and leaves fragments like http or tco.
  3. Remove @mentions (@\w+): Removes airline handles (@united, @VirginAmerica) BEFORE punctuation removal so the model learns sentiment rather than airline identity.
  4. Unwrap Hashtags (#(\w+) → \1): Drops # while keeping the meaningful word (#delayed → delayed).
  5. Remove Numbers & Punctuation ([^a-z\s] → ' '): Removes digits, punctuation, and emojis to keep a clean alphabetic vocabulary.
  6. Collapse Extra Spaces (\s+ → ' '): Normalises multiple spaces/tabs/newlines into single spaces.

Information Lost Warning: Removing punctuation and non-ASCII symbols strips useful sentiment cues such as repeated exclamation marks ("awful!!!"), all-caps shouting ("WORST"), and expressive emojis (😡, ❤️). We keep raw text for VADER (Task 3.3) precisely for this reason.

print("URL removal      :", re.sub(r"https?://\S+", " ", sample_url))
print("Mention removal  :", re.sub(r"@\w+", " ", sample_mention))
print("Hashtag unwrap   :", re.sub(r"#(\w+)", r"\1", sample_hashtag))
print("Hashtags found   :", re.findall(r"#(\w+)", sample_hashtag))
print("Only letters     :", re.sub(r"[^a-z\s]", " ", sample_punct_num.lower()))
print("Collapse spaces  :", re.sub(r"\s+", " ", sample_spaces).strip())

URL removal      : Check status at   or   now
Mention removal  :     why is my gate changed?
Hashtag unwrap   : Still waiting delayed WorstAirlineEver
Hashtags found   : ['delayed', 'WorstAirlineEver']
Only letters     : flight     delayed   hrs    unacceptable

Pattern Meaning of Each Symbol Example Match
https?://\S+ https + optional s (?) + :// + one or more non-whitespace chars (\S+) https://t.co/abc123
@\w+ Literal @ followed by one or more word characters (a-zA-Z0-9_) @VirginAmerica
#(\w+) Literal # followed by capturing group (\w+) reused via \1 #delayed → delayed
[^a-z\s] Negated character class matching anything NOT a lowercase letter or whitespace 402, !, .
\s+ One or more whitespace characters (spaces, tabs, newlines) " " → " "

Why Keeping Negation Words Matters (Task 2.4):
Standard English stop-word lists contain not, no, nor, and never. Removing them blindly turns "not happy with the delay" into ["happy", "delay"]—which flips a clear complaint into something that looks partially positive! Preserving negation words keeps the sentiment inversion intact for downstream features and models.

Vocabulary Observations & Task 4 Settings (Task 2.5):

  • Surprising tokens: flightled (a dataset anonymisation/stemming artifact of "cancelled"), amp (HTML entity &amp; after stripping punctuation), and thanks appearing even inside negative tweets (often sarcastic like "thanks for nothing" or polite closings "please help thanks").
  • Guiding min_df & max_features: Over half of the cleaned vocabulary consists of words appearing only once (typos, rare names, random strings). Setting min_df=2 filters out single-occurrence noise, while capping max_features (e.g., 5000) focuses the model on informative recurring words without memory bloat.

Task 3: Different NLP Approaches — Heuristic & API-Based¶

  • Objective: Implement and evaluate two non-ML baselines—a custom domain heuristic lexicon and NLTK's VADER engine—on the exact same stratified test split that ML models will use later.
  • Expected Output: Conceptual comparison of all 3 approaches, heuristic lexicon results on 5 sample tweets, VADER evaluation, side-by-side test metrics/confusion matrices, and 4 analysed failure cases.

3.1 Comparing the Three NLP Approach Families¶

Dimension 1. Heuristic (Rules & Lexicon) 2. API-Based (Ready-Made Engine) 3. Machine Learning (Trained on Data)
How it works Hand-written word lists + explicit rules (e.g., negation window). Send text to a pre-built engine (VADER or Cloud API) and read scores. Learn word weights automatically from labelled examples.
Advantages Zero training data needed; fast; 100% interpretable and offline. Instant setup; handles slang/punctuation/emojis out of the box. Learns domain jargon (flightled, gate, hold) and subtle patterns; highest accuracy.
Disadvantages Brittle on sarcasm, synonyms, and unseen words; manual upkeep. No domain adaptation; Cloud APIs incur per-call cost and latency/privacy risk. Requires labelled dataset; less transparent than simple word lists.
When to choose in a company Strict offline/privacy rules, tiny budget, no labelled data yet. Quick MVP prototype when budget allows API calls and data isn't sensitive. Production classifier when labelled history exists and high macro-F1 matters.

In [10]:
# Task 3.3: API-based approach using NLTK VADER on raw tweets
vader = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer()

def vader_sentiment(raw_text: str) -> str:
    comp = vader.polarity_scores(str(raw_text))["compound"]
    if comp >= 0.05:
        return "positive"
    elif comp <= -0.05:
        return "negative"
    return "neutral"

print("Sample VADER compound scores on the 5 hand-picked tweets:")
for tw in sample_5:
    scores = vader.polarity_scores(tw)
    print(f"{vader_sentiment(tw).upper():8s} (compound={scores['compound']:+.3f}) -> {tw}")

How Cloud NLP APIs Work (Task 3.3):
Managed cloud services such as Google Cloud Natural Language, AWS Comprehend, and Microsoft Azure Text Analytics follow the exact same request-response pattern demonstrated above with VADER: your application sends raw text over HTTPS and receives a JSON payload containing sentiment labels and confidence/polarity scores. Because cloud services require an account, API keys, and billing—and introduce external network dependencies—we describe them conceptually here and run VADER locally as our reproducible API-style baseline.

def evaluate_predictions(name, y_true, y_pred, train_time=0.0):
    labels = ["negative", "neutral", "positive"]
    acc = accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred)
    mf1 = f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average="macro")
    prec_neg = precision_score(y_true, y_pred, labels=labels, average=None)[0]
    rec_pos = recall_score(y_true, y_pred, labels=labels, average=None)[2]
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, labels=labels)
    return {
        "Approach": name,
        "Accuracy": acc,
        "Macro-F1": mf1,
        "Precision (negative)": prec_neg,
        "Recall (positive)": rec_pos,
        "Train Time (s)": train_time,
        "cm": cm,
        "report": classification_report(y_true, y_pred, labels=labels, digits=3),
    }

y_pred_heur = X_test_raw.apply(heuristic_sentiment)
y_pred_vader = X_test_raw.apply(vader_sentiment)

res_heur = evaluate_predictions("Heuristic (Domain Lexicon)", y_test, y_pred_heur)
res_vader = evaluate_predictions("API-Based (NLTK VADER)", y_test, y_pred_vader)

summary_t3 = pd.DataFrame([
    {k: v for k, v in r.items() if k not in ("cm", "report")}
    for r in [res_heur, res_vader]
])

Why Rules and General-Purpose Tools Fail (Task 3.5):

  • Heuristic failures happen when a tweet complains without using one of our 38 negative words (e.g., phrasing like "left on tarmac with no water") or uses sarcasm where a positive keyword appears without an explicit negation.
  • VADER failures happen because VADER is a general social-media lexicon that does not strongly penalise airline-domain tokens such as cancelled, flightled, hold, or baggage when no emotional adjectives appear, or misreads polite phrases ("please help").
  • Conclusion: General rules cannot capture domain-specific phrasing and context weights automatically—we need machine learning models trained directly on labelled airline tweets.

Task 4: Feature Extraction — Bag-of-Words, TF-IDF & N-Grams¶

  • Objective: Convert variable-length text into fixed-length numeric vectors, verify BoW and TF-IDF mathematics manually against scikit-learn, and measure vocabulary growth across ngram_range and max_features.
  • Expected Output: Comparison table, manual vs sklearn verification (np.allclose), train-only vectoriser statistics, top negative/positive bigrams, and feature-size memory chart.

4.1 Why Feature Extraction? BoW vs TF-IDF vs N-Grams¶

Machine-learning classifiers compute dot products and probabilities over fixed-length numeric vectors—they cannot consume raw strings directly.

| Technique | What It Captures | What It Ignores | Vector Size | Sparsity | Typical Weakness | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Bag-of-Words (BoW) | Raw frequency of each individual word in the document. | Word order, grammar, and semantic similarity. | |V| (thousands of words) | Very high (>99% zeros) | Common filler words dominate counts; "not good" = "good not". | | TF-IDF | Word importance: frequent in this tweet, rare across the corpus. | Word order and synonym meaning. | |V| (thousands of words) | Very high (>99% zeros) | Still treats each word independently; ignores multi-word negation. | | N-Grams (e.g., Bigrams) | Short consecutive word phrases (not happy, customer service). | Long-range dependencies beyond n words and synonyms. | Huge (|V| grows rapidly with n) | Extremely high (>99.8% zeros) | Vocabulary explosion, memory overhead, and overfitting on rare phrases. |

In [13]:

Why 'the movie was good, not bad' and 'the movie was bad, not good' Are Hard to Separate with BoW (Task 4.2):
Unigram Bag-of-Words treats a document as an unordered multiset of single words. Both sentences contain the exact same seven words (the, movie, was, good, not, bad), so they produce identical BoW vectors even though their meanings are opposites.

Why Default TfidfVectorizer() Differs & Why Common Words Get Low Weight (Task 4.3):

  1. Two Differences in Default TfidfVectorizer(): (a) smooth_idf=True uses $\text{idf} = \ln\left(\frac{N + 1}{\text{df} + 1}\right) + 1$, pretending an extra document contains every word to prevent zero divisions; (b) norm='l2' scales each row vector to unit Euclidean length ($\|\mathbf{x}\|_2 = 1$) so long tweets do not overpower short ones.
  2. Low Weight for Ubiquitous Words: When a word appears in every document ($\text{df} = N$), $\ln(N/N) + 1 = 1$, which is the smallest possible IDF multiplier—correctly down-weighting filler words like "the" or "flight" that carry little class-discriminating signal.
In [15]:
# Task 4.4: BoW and TF-IDF fitted on TRAINING clean_text ONLY
def inspect_matrix(name, vec, X_tr, X_te):
    nnz = X_tr.nnz
    total_cells = X_tr.shape[0] * X_tr.shape[1]
    sparsity = 100.0 * (1.0 - nnz / total_cells)
    print(f"{name:32s} | Train: {X_tr.shape} | Test: {X_te.shape} | Vocab: {len(vec.vocabulary_):5d} | NNZ: {nnz:7d} | Sparsity: {sparsity:.3f}%")

cv_full = CountVectorizer()
X_tr_bow = cv_full.fit_transform(X_train_text)
X_te_bow = cv_full.transform(X_test_text)

tf_full = TfidfVectorizer()
X_tr_tf = tf_full.fit_transform(X_train_text)
X_te_tf = tf_full.transform(X_test_text)

tf_pruned = TfidfVectorizer(min_df=2, max_features=5000)
X_tr_tf_p = tf_pruned.fit_transform(X_train_text)
X_te_tf_p = tf_pruned.transform(X_test_text)

inspect_matrix("CountVectorizer (full)", cv_full, X_tr_bow, X_te_bow)
inspect_matrix("TfidfVectorizer (full)", tf_full, X_tr_tf, X_te_tf)
inspect_matrix("TfidfVectorizer (min_df=2,5k)", tf_pruned, X_tr_tf_p, X_te_tf_p)

Why Vectorisers Must Be Fitted on Training Data Only (Task 4.4):
Fitting a vectoriser on the full dataset leaks test-set vocabulary and inverse-document-frequency (IDF) statistics into training. In real deployment, unseen test/user tweets are unknown during training—fitting only on X_train keeps evaluation honest and prevents optimistic data leakage.

Bigram Meaning & Cost of Larger n (Task 4.5):

  • Two examples where bigrams carry meaning lost by unigrams: (1) customer service captures a specific airline department frequently criticised or praised, whereas customer and service alone are ambiguous; (2) on hold / not happy capture waiting frustration or negated sentiment that single words miss.
  • Cost of larger n: Moving from unigrams to bigrams and trigrams multiplies vocabulary size dramatically, increasing matrix memory, training time, and sparsity—many trigrams occur only a handful of times and risk overfitting.

Choosing a Sensible Setting (Task 4.6):
ngram_range=(1, 2) with min_df=2 (around ~13k features, < 2 MB sparse data) captures critical phrases like not happy and customer service while avoiding the trigram vocabulary explosion. When stricter memory limits apply, max_features=5000–10000 keeps nearly all high-signal terms at a fraction of the footprint.

Task 5: Word Embeddings, Word2Vec — CBoW & Skip-gram¶

  • Objective: Train both CBoW and Skip-gram Word2Vec models on training tweets, inspect learned word similarities and 2-D PCA clusters, and build averaged dense document vectors for classification.
  • Expected Output: CBoW vs Skip-gram comparison with window example, training stats, 6-word similarity table, 3 cosine similarities, 60-word PCA plot, and X_train_w2v / X_test_w2v.

5.1 Why Word Embeddings?¶

BoW and TF-IDF treat every word as an independent one-hot column: delayed and late are completely orthogonal with zero mathematical similarity. Word embeddings instead represent each word as a compact dense vector (for example 100 real numbers) learned from surrounding word contexts—capturing the distributional principle "a word is known by the company it keeps" (J. R. Firth) so words appearing in similar contexts end up close together in vector space.

5.2 CBoW vs Skip-gram¶

Property Continuous Bag-of-Words (CBoW, sg=0) Skip-gram (sg=1)
Input Surrounding context words within window Single centre target word
Output Predicted centre word Predicted surrounding context words
Training Speed Faster (averages context into one update) Slower (updates for each context pair)
Frequent Words Strong, smooth representations Good, slightly slower to converge
Rare Words Weaker (rare words get smoothed out) Stronger (each appearance generates multiple pairs)
When to Prefer Larger datasets where speed matters Smaller corpora or tasks where rare sentiment words matter

Worked Window Example (window = 2) on "the flight was delayed again"¶

  • CBoW (context → centre) pairs:
    • (["flight", "was"], "the")
    • (["the", "was", "delayed"], "flight")
    • (["the", "flight", "delayed", "again"], "was")
    • (["flight", "was", "again"], "delayed")
    • (["was", "delayed"], "again")
  • Skip-gram (centre → context) pairs:
    • "the" → "flight", "was"
    • "flight" → "the", "was", "delayed"
    • "was" → "the", "flight", "delayed", "again"
    • "delayed" → "flight", "was", "again"
    • "again" → "was", "delayed"
In [18]:
# Task 5.3: Train CBoW (sg=0) and Skip-gram (sg=1) on TRAINING tokens only
train_tokens = [s.split() for s in X_train_text]
test_tokens = [s.split() for s in X_test_text]

t0 = time.perf_counter()
w2v_cbow = Word2Vec(
    sentences=train_tokens,
    vector_size=100,
    window=5,
    min_count=3,
    sg=0,
    epochs=20,
    seed=42,
    workers=1,
)
cbow_time = time.perf_counter() - t0

Honest Vector Assessment (Task 5.4):
Overall the neighbours are domain-sensible (delayed pairs with late/cancelled, thanks pairs with thank/appreciate, luggage pairs with baggage/bags). Skip-gram gives slightly sharper semantic groupings on less frequent complaint words (rude, luggage) than CBoW. However, because our training split contains only ~11.5k short tweets (roughly 150k–200k tokens total), these embeddings are noticeably noisier than models trained on billion-word corpora.

Even in 2 dimensions, related words group together: gratitude words (thanks, thank, great, love), time/delay complaint words (hours, delayed, cancelled, wait, hold), and operational nouns (flight, plane, gate, bag) cluster in distinct regions, while common function words sit near the origin.

In [21]:
# Task 5.6: Document vectors via averaging (using Skip-gram based on Task 5.4)
def doc_vector(tokens, model):
    vecs = [model.wv[t] for t in tokens if t in model.wv]
    if not vecs:
        return np.zeros(model.vector_size, dtype=np.float32)
    return np.mean(vecs, axis=0)

X_train_w2v = np.vstack([doc_vector(toks, w2v_sg) for toks in train_tokens])
X_test_w2v = np.vstack([doc_vector(toks, w2v_sg) for toks in test_tokens])

print("X_train_w2v shape:", X_train_w2v.shape)
print("X_test_w2v shape :", X_test_w2v.shape)

X_train_w2v shape: (11541, 100)
X_test_w2v shape : (2886, 100)

What Information Is Lost When Averaging Word Vectors (Task 5.6):
Simple vector averaging discards word order and syntax (so "not good" and "good not" average to the same point) and dilutes strong sentiment words by mixing them equally with high-frequency neutral filler words (the, to, flight, my).

Task 6: Text Classification Pipeline & Approach Comparison¶

  • Objective: Train and compare ML classifiers across BoW, TF-IDF, N-grams, and Word2Vec inside leak-free scikit-learn Pipeline objects, compare all NLP approaches in one chart/table, validate via 5-fold CV, analyse errors, and save sentiment_model.joblib.
  • Expected Output: Baseline pipeline evaluation, 6-model comparison table, all-approach comparison chart, 5-fold CV check, 8 misclassified tweets analysed, and verified joblib model reload.

6.1 Text Classification & Why Pipeline Matters¶

Text classification assigns a single discrete category (negative, neutral, or positive) to an entire document. In our project, the classification pipeline flows as:
raw tweet → clean_text() → vectoriser (TF-IDF / BoW) → classifier (Logistic Regression) → predicted sentiment & probabilities → macro-F1 evaluation.

Wrapping the vectoriser and classifier inside a scikit-learn Pipeline guarantees two critical protections:

  1. Zero Data Leakage: Calling pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train) or cross_val_score(pipeline, ...) automatically fits the vocabulary and IDF weights strictly inside each training fold and only transforms validation/test folds.
  2. One-File Deployment: Saving the Pipeline with joblib bundles both the fitted vocabulary/IDF weights and the classifier weights into a single .joblib object so app.py only needs model.predict([cleaned_text]).
In [22]:

Why class_weight='balanced' for This Dataset? (Task 6.2):
With 63% negative vs 16% positive tweets, an unweighted classifier minimizes overall loss by favouring the majority negative class. Setting class_weight='balanced' scales each class's loss inversely proportional to its training frequency, boosting recall on minority neutral and positive tweets and directly raising Macro-F1.

Ranking & Deployment Decision (Task 6.4):

  1. ML with TF-IDF Unigrams+Bigrams (Logistic Regression / LinearSVC) leads by a large margin, followed by TF-IDF Unigrams and BoW, then Word2Vec averaged vectors, VADER, and finally the hand-built Heuristic.
  2. Why: TF-IDF unigrams+bigrams learns exact domain weights (flightled, not happy, on hold, thanks) while down-weighting generic terms (flight). Word2Vec averaging lags behind sparse n-grams because averaging washes out negation and sharp keywords in short tweets. VADER lacks airline-specific penalties, and our 76-word heuristic has limited coverage.
  3. Deployment Choice: We deploy TF-IDF (1,2) + LogisticRegression(class_weight='balanced') because it delivers top-tier Macro-F1 (~0.73+), runs in milliseconds, and natively outputs calibrated class probabilities (predict_proba) for the Streamlit confidence bar chart.

Cross-Validation Interpretation (Task 6.5):
The 5-fold CV mean Macro-F1 closely matches the held-out test Macro-F1 (gap < 0.02), confirming that our pipeline generalises stably without overfitting. A large positive gap (e.g., CV much higher than test) would indicate overfitting to training noise or subtle data leakage.

Error Patterns & Two Concrete In-Scope Improvements (Task 6.6):

  • Observed Patterns: (1) neutral tweets mentioning delays or customer service questions get pulled into negative; (2) sarcastic negative tweets containing polite words (thanks, great) get predicted as positive; (3) very short tweets (2-4 words) lack enough n-gram evidence.
  • Two In-Scope Improvements:
    1. Tune TfidfVectorizer with sublinear_tf=True and include ngram_range=(1, 3) with max_features=20000 (via cross-validation on X_train only) to catch 3-word sarcastic/negated idioms like "thanks for nothing".
    2. Tune the Logistic Regression regularisation parameter C via 5-fold CV on the training split to better calibrate the boundary between neutral inquiries and negative complaints.

Task 7: POS Tagging¶

  • Objective: Understand how Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging resolves word ambiguity using context, inspect NLTK tagger accuracy on informal tweets, visualise POS distributions by sentiment, and test whether keeping only content-sentiment POS tags helps TF-IDF classification.
  • Expected Output: POS tag reference and ambiguity explanation, 5 tagged tweets + 2 ambiguity sentences with error analysis, POS distribution grouped bar chart across 2,000 tweets, top 10 adjectives per class, and POS-filtered pipeline comparison.

7.1 What Is POS Tagging & Why Is It Useful?¶

Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging assigns each word in a sentence its grammatical category based on both its definition and surrounding context. Common Penn Treebank tags include:

Word Type Penn Treebank Code(s) Example
Noun NN, NNS, NNP flight, bags, United
Verb VB, VBD, VBG, VBN delay, delayed, waiting
Adjective JJ, JJR, JJS rude, better, worst
Adverb RB, RBR, RBS never, very, extremely
Pronoun PRP, PRP$ I, they, my
Preposition IN on, at, with

POS tagging helps NLP systems perform word-sense disambiguation, information extraction (pulling nouns/entities), grammar checking, and feature engineering (isolating adjectives/adverbs that carry opinion).

7.2 How POS Tagging Works¶

  1. Rule-Based Tagger: Uses a dictionary of possible tags per word plus hand-written contextual rules (e.g., "if the previous word is the, tag the next ambiguous word as a noun").
  2. Statistical / Machine-Learning Tagger: Learns from a manually tagged corpus the probability or feature weights of a tag given the target word, suffixes, capitalisation, and neighbouring tags (e.g., Hidden Markov Models or an averaged perceptron).
  3. Resolving Ambiguity via Context: Look at the word book in two sentences:
    • "I will **book** a ticket tomorrow." → book follows modal "will" (MD), so it is tagged as a verb (VB).
    • "I read a **book** during the flight." → book follows article "a" (DT), so it is tagged as a noun (NN).

NLTK's nltk.pos_tag() uses a trained averaged-perceptron model (averaged_perceptron_tagger_eng), which was trained primarily on formal news-style text (Wall Street Journal / Penn Treebank).

In [28]:

Why Tweets Are Harder for pos_tag Than News (Task 7.3):
Because NLTK's averaged perceptron was trained on formal, properly capitalised and punctuated Wall Street Journal sentences, it frequently mis-tags informal lowercase tweets (e.g., tagging lowercase proper nouns or slang/typos like vx, plz, or flightled as common nouns NN or misreading imperatives without punctuation/capitalisation like "please/VB" vs "thanks/NNS").

POS Distribution Observations (Task 7.4):

  • Positive tweets exhibit a noticeably higher share of adjectives (JJ*) such as great, good, best, awesome, and friendly because praise directly modifies the flight experience.
  • Negative tweets use slightly more verbs (VB*) and adverbs (RB*) (not, never, still, waiting, cancelled) as passengers narrate what went wrong.
  • Neutral tweets show the highest proportion of nouns (NN*), consistent with factual questions about flights, gates, seats, and schedules.

# Task 7.5: POS-filtered features (JJ*, RB*, VB*, and negation words) vs Full-text pipeline
def pos_filter_text(text: str) -> str:
    tokens = nltk.word_tokenize(text)
    tagged = nltk.pos_tag(tokens)
    kept = [
        w for w, tag in tagged
        if tag.startswith(("JJ", "RB", "VB")) or w in NEGATION_WORDS
    ]
    return " ".join(kept)

X_train_pos = X_train_text.apply(pos_filter_text)
X_test_pos = X_test_text.apply(pos_filter_text)

pos_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("tfidf", TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=2)),
    ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced", random_state=RANDOM_STATE)),
])
pos_pipe.fit(X_train_pos, y_train)
y_pred_pos = pos_pipe.predict(X_test_pos)
res_pos = evaluate_predictions("POS-Filtered TF-IDF (1,2) + LR", y_test, y_pred_pos)

pos_comp = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Pipeline": "Full-Text TF-IDF (1,2) + LR", "Accuracy": res_base["Accuracy"], "Macro-F1": res_base["Macro-F1"]},
    {"Pipeline": "POS-Filtered (JJ/RB/VB + Neg) TF-IDF (1,2) + LR", "Accuracy": res_pos["Accuracy"], "Macro-F1": res_pos["Macro-F1"]},
])
display(pos_comp.round(4))

Did POS Filtering Help, Hurt, or Make No Difference? (Task 7.5):
POS filtering slightly hurt Macro-F1 compared to the full-text pipeline. Dropping nouns and prepositions removes critical airline-domain clues (such as luggage, baggage, hold, hours, refund, customer service) and causes NLTK tagger errors on noisy lowercase tweets to discard genuine sentiment words. Full-text TF-IDF retains all domain nouns and multi-word phrases.

What the user sees after pressing Predict:
The app validates and cleans the input using the shared clean_text() from nlp_utils.py, displays a coloured sentiment banner (st.success for positive, st.warning for neutral, st.error for negative), renders the cleaned text alongside the selected approach's breakdown (for the ML model, a class-probability st.bar_chart; for VADER, polarity breakdown; for Heuristic, matched lexicon words and negation flips), and provides a collapsible st.expander displaying NLTK POS tags.

8.8 What I Learned (Reflection)¶

  1. Which pipeline stage had the biggest effect on accuracy: Moving from generic rules/VADER to domain-trained feature extraction (TF-IDF unigrams + bigrams) paired with class_weight='balanced' produced the largest jump in Macro-F1, because the model learned airline-specific negative phrases (flightled, on hold, customer service) and balanced predictions across minority classes.
  2. Which approach I deployed and why: I deployed TF-IDF (1,2) + LogisticRegression(class_weight='balanced') (sentiment_model.joblib), while keeping Heuristic and VADER selectable in the app for live comparison, because the ML pipeline achieved the highest Macro-F1 (~0.74), handles negation bigrams well, and provides calibrated probabilities.
  3. One weakness a user could notice: Subtle sarcasm (e.g., "Great job leaving my bags in Chicago!") can still fool linear n-gram weights because the words "great" and "job" carry strong positive weights across the training set.
  4. One improvement beyond this practical's scope: Replacing bag-of-n-grams with a pre-trained Transformer model (such as BERT or RoBERTa fine-tuned on tweets) to capture long-range contextual sarcasm and word order—named here only as future work.
